uncited: *   **Inputs:** Ray origin, ray direction, medium definition (density, optical depth, phase function), light description (position, direction, falloff), and shadow map data.
*   **Light Volume Geometry:** Defined by front faces ($G_f$) and back faces ($G_b$).
These define the integration intervals along the ray.
**Interval Decomposition:** Identify the intersection points of the view ray with the light volume.
*   **Directional Lights:** Assume constant direction and constant power (light distance $\gg$ medium depth).
*   **Omnidirectional Lights:** Due to complexity, terms are expressed with respect to direction and distance.
A lookup texture mapping $\cos^{-1}(v \cdot l)$ is created.
*   **Spot Lights:** The angular falloff complicates the integral.
The interval must be clamped to the cone intersection.
*   *No Falloff:* Treated as a point light.
*   *Fixed Falloff:* Use a modified point light LUT.
*   **Shadow Map Inconsistencies:** If only front faces are rendered to the shadow map, or if distant occluders are excluded, the integration intervals may be incorrect, causing visible artifacts.
*   **Temporal Jitter:** Temporal AA jitter can cause flickering in down-sampled buffers because a 1-pixel flicker at full resolution can become a 4x4 pixel artifact in a 1/4 resolution buffer.
*   **High-Frequency Occluders:** Dense occluders at low viewing angles (e.g., sunset through woods) cause performance drops due to high pixel coverage.
*   **Time Complexity:** Depends on the number of light volume intersections and the complexity of the light solver.
This method was developed by NVIDIA for use in *Fallout 4*, integrating with their Gameworks volumetric lighting system.
